extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy / classical political theory
extracted.subtask_description: Interpretation and normative account of the origins, nature, and organisation of the city (polis) and household—including family relations, slavery, property, and household economy—from Aristotle's Politics. Focuses on what constitutes good government and proper management of household affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: City as the natural and perfect form of government
rubrics_metrics.description: A city is the work of nature and contains in itself the end and perfection of government: first founded that we might live, but continued that we may live happily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle treats the city as the final cause of subordinate societies; the whole (city) is prior to its parts (families, individuals). The best state is one which attains the final cause—living well—not merely surviving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Man as a political animal (speech and justice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Man is naturally a political animal; speech proves that man is more social than other animals because through speech we express what is just and unjust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speech enables the perception and communication of good/evil and just/unjust; participation in these common sentiments forms families and the city. The capacity for determining rightness distinguishes humans from other animals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of the whole over parts in defining nature
rubrics_metrics.description: The notion of a city naturally precedes that of a family or an individual, because the whole must necessarily be prior to the parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle argues by appeal to 'energic qualities': when the active powers of a thing cease, it cannot be considered the same; thus political wholes define the identity and purpose of their parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Household composition: three distinct parts
rubrics_metrics.description: A complete family consists of freemen and slaves and is composed of three distinct parts: the master and slave (herile), the husband and wife (nuptial), and the father and child (paternal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle proposes to examine these three relationships separately to understand the nature and proper governance of the household.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature and justification of slavery (natural slavery)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some men are slaves by nature: those who lack the rational capacity and are best used as 'animated instruments' for others are naturally suited to be slaves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle claims that where slavery is advantageous it can be just; he appeals to analogy (soul governing body) and asserts some persons are by their nature fit to be governed. He acknowledges controversy and aims to distinguish natural slavery from slavery by law/conquest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between slavery by nature and slavery by law/conquest
rubrics_metrics.description: Slavery may arise naturally or by compact/law (e.g., prisoners taken in war); slavery imposed by force may be challenged as unjust, and the legal right to enslave does not automatically make it just in all cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle recognises debate: some argue slavery by conquest is unjust because force alone should not determine moral status. He suggests distinguishing those who are naturally slaves from those enslaved by circumstance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of mastery: employing slaves vs mere possession
rubrics_metrics.description: The master is so called not merely from possession but from the capacity to employ slaves appropriately; the master's knowledge is to order, the slave's knowledge is to perform particular household tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mastery is a practical skill—knowing how to order household affairs and employ servants—rather than a high intellectual virtue. Those who can avoid these low attentions appoint stewards and pursue public or philosophical life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slave as animated instrument; property as instrument for use
rubrics_metrics.description: A slave is a particular species of property — an animated instrument whose services are 'for use'; possessions function as instruments distinct from that of making/producing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle analyses 'use' vs 'making' to classify possessions: instruments effect something else, whereas used goods (beds, coats) are used. A slave is considered part-like in function (used by the master) though not a mere part of the master's body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy (household management) vs money-getting (pecuniary acquisition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The art of managing a household (economy) is distinct from the art of getting money; natural acquisition (for subsistence) has limits, whereas pecuniary acquisition (trade, hoarding money) is potentially limitless and not in accordance with nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economy aims to procure what is necessary for a good life and has boundaries; money-getting for its own sake is criticized as wanting an infinite increase and subverting the ends of proper household management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural acquisition (provision) as proper part of economy
rubrics_metrics.description: Acquisition according to nature—procurement of subsistence (food, produce, animals)—is part of economy and is necessary and bounded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle treats provision methods like farming, hunting, and husbandry as natural modes of subsistence; barter may emerge naturally when communities enlarge, and certain forms of acquisition (those serving life and the household) are proper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pecuniary acquisition and the origins of money and trade
rubrics_metrics.description: Barter introduced exchange and led to the invention of money as a convenient medium; the art of money-getting chiefly concerns trade—finding where greatest profits can be made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Money is an artificial convention whose value depends on common agreement; commerce allows indefinite accumulation of wealth, unlike natural economy, and money-getting thus falls outside the bounded ends of household management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usury is against nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Usury — 'breeding' money from money — is most against nature and is the worst form of money-getting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle argues usury increases money by money itself rather than employing it for exchange; it treats money as productive in itself (tokos) and thus contradicts natural ends of economic activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical arts of domestic management are proper and commendable
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge of the most profitable livestock, agriculture, apiculture, fishing, and metallurgy are proper parts of household management and useful to those who attend to getting provision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle notes practical manuals exist for these arts; the best works are those where chance has least to do, and the meanest employments are those that most deprave the body and require mere manual labour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods of commercial money-making (merchandise, usury, wages)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three chief ways of gaining money by exchange: sending commodities for sale (merchandise), usury, and receiving wages for work (either craft or labour).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merchandise may vary by safety and profit (sea vs land, selling at source), wages depend on manual or low-skilled labour; Aristotle situates these practices relative to natural economy and criticizes those divorced from natural ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monopoly and political uses of money-getting
rubrics_metrics.description: Monopolising commodities (e.g., Thales' olive-press monopoly, buying up iron supply) is an effective way to raise money and is sometimes used by private individuals and cities to acquire wealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle gives examples where monopolistic contrivances yielded great profit; politicians may employ such means to raise public funds, though some rulers may forbid practices deemed inconsistent with civic affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domestic government is monarchical; political state is rule of free equals
rubrics_metrics.description: Domestic (household) government is essentially a monarchy (one ruler), while a political state is the government of free men and equals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle distinguishes forms appropriate to the household (one master) from those appropriate to the city (free citizens governing/being governed); the nature of persons governed (slaves vs free) demands different governmental forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different governance for wives and children within the household
rubrics_metrics.description: The governance of the wife and of the children should both be that of free persons but not the same: the wife should be treated as a citizen of a free state, while children should be under kingly power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle posits a natural hierarchy (male superior to female except in unusual cases; elder/perfect to younger/imperfect) and recommends different modes and forms (distinctions in forms, expressions, honours) for the relations within the household.
